standard.title: Acquire, store and validate data
standard.description: develop techniques to acquire, store and validate data from a range of sources using software, including spreadsheets and databases
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can acquire, store and validate data from a range of sources using spreadsheets and databases (AC9TDI8P01). They can identify data quality issues including relevance, correctness, currency and potential bias. They have not yet developed automated validation techniques, applied the Australian Privacy Principles to data collection, or considered training data issues for predictive models.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students develop techniques — including automated validation, privacy-compliant acquisition, and bias-aware evaluation — to acquire, store and validate data from a range of sources using spreadsheets and databases.

nodes.label: Designing systems that collect structured data
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can design and develop a system that collects structured data from users, with appropriate fields and data types.
nodes.minimum_width: Design and build a data collection form or interface that captures at least two data types (e.g. numeric rating and text comment); store collected data in a structured format.
nodes.typical_width: Design a data collection system for a specific purpose (e.g. a review or feedback system); define appropriate field types, required fields, and storage format; explain how the structure supports later analysis.
wider: Design a data collection system for a community need (e.g. event feedback, local environment monitoring) and consider what structural decisions support the community's analytical needs
Compare how different Likert scale configurations (3-point vs 5-point vs 7-point) affect the quality of data collected and what statistical operations become possible

response_modes.reason: Data collection system design requires students to reason from the analytical question backward to field types and schema — students who jump to implementation without this reasoning produce ad-hoc schemas that cannot be validated or analysed. The scaffold: question → required data → field types → storage structure.

success_criteria: Data collection system captures at least two distinct data types
Collected data is stored in a structured format accessible for analysis
nodes.hinge_reason: Poorly designed data collection structure cascades through N2, N3 and N4 — automated validation cannot be built on an undefined schema, privacy compliance cannot be assessed without knowing what data is collected, and source comparison is meaningless without a clear collection target.

nodes.label: Automated validation techniques
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop automated validation techniques that check data is correct and meaningful using both rules and UI constraints.
nodes.minimum_width: Implement at least one automated validation rule (e.g. input range constraint, data type check, or required field check) and explain what it prevents.
nodes.typical_width: Implement multiple validation techniques — UI element constraints, rule-based checks, and at least one statistical technique (e.g. detecting outliers or inconsistent ratings); explain what each technique catches and what it cannot catch.
wider: Implement validation that detects potential bias in collected responses (e.g. all 5-star reviews from a single IP address) and explain the statistical reasoning
Investigate how automated content moderation systems combine rule-based and ML-based validation — what each approach handles well and where each fails
Consider training data issues such as the zero problem — what happens when a predictive model has no training examples for a valid input category, and how validation can surface this

response_modes.reason: Validation design requires students to reason from the threat (what could go wrong?) to the check (how would we detect it?) to the implementation. Without this reasoning scaffold, students implement surface-level checks without thinking about what attack or error each check addresses.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The statistical bias detection and ML training data directions connect validation to consequential real-world systems — AI model outputs, fake review detection. These are substantive extensions for advancing students.
success_criteria: Implements at least one automated validation rule that prevents an identifiable class of bad data
Explains what the rule catches and at least one case it would not catch
nodes.hinge_reason: Unvalidated data renders downstream analysis unreliable — students who cannot implement validation collect data they cannot trust, and any privacy compliance decisions or source comparisons built on bad data produce meaningless conclusions.

nodes.label: Privacy-compliant data acquisition
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can acquire and store data in accordance with the Australian Privacy Principles, protecting personally identifiable information from unauthorised access.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one personally identifiable element in a data collection system and explain what the Australian Privacy Principles require for that data.
nodes.typical_width: Design a data collection system that acquires data according to the Australian Privacy Principles — limiting collection to what is necessary, protecting PII from public exposure, and ensuring data is not shared without consent; explain the specific APP requirements applied.
wider: Evaluate an existing data collection system (e.g. a school app, community platform) against the Australian Privacy Principles — identify gaps and recommend improvements
Investigate how systems collecting data from or about First Nations Australians must also address Indigenous data sovereignty principles, and how these extend beyond the APPs
Compare how data protection requirements differ across jurisdictions (APPs in Australia, GDPR in Europe) and explain the implications for systems used globally

response_modes.reason: Privacy compliance is abstract without concrete cases. Students need to apply APP requirements to different data types — health data, location data, contact data — to understand how the principles operate in practice rather than as a compliance checklist.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Indigenous data sovereignty adds a substantive layer beyond the APPs — it is not just an enrichment topic but a genuine second framework with different principles. The comparison with GDPR is similarly rich.
success_criteria: Identifies at least one personally identifiable data element in a system
Explains at least one APP requirement that applies to that data and how the system satisfies or violates it

nodes.label: Comparing and selecting data sources
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the strengths and weaknesses of different data collection methods and select sources appropriate to a given investigation.
nodes.minimum_width: Given a research question, identify two different data collection methods and describe one strength and one weakness of each.
nodes.typical_width: Compare at least three data collection methods (e.g. online survey, observation, existing dataset such as ABS); explain how each method's strengths and weaknesses affect its suitability for a specific question; select the most appropriate method and justify.
wider: Access and store ABS population data in a format suitable for analysis; evaluate what questions the dataset can and cannot answer
Investigate how browser history, phone logs or social media data are collected passively — compare this to consent-based collection and evaluate the ethical difference
Design a mixed-method data collection approach that compensates for the weaknesses of each individual method

response_modes.reason: Students default to surveys. Broader exposure to source types — existing datasets, observation, passive collection, interviews — builds a more complete picture of the data acquisition landscape and what each method is and isn't suited for.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two data collection methods and a specific strength and weakness of each
Justifies selection of a method for a specific investigation with reference to its strengths relative to the question
